title: Build a REST API With a Real SQLite Database — Full Node.js + Express + Jest Capstone Walkthrough
description:
This is the Level 3 capstone of the JavaScript Mastery Path, built one file at a time: a Book Catalog API with full CRUD, backed by a real SQLite database file, with centralized error handling and a Jest plus supertest suite covering every route. We walk through the project layout, the package.json toolchain, the database setup in db.js, a controller that prepares its SQL once and validates input into an errors array, the Express router that maps every HTTP verb to a controller call and hands failures off to one error handler, the app wiring with its 404 and 500 safety nets, the tiny server entry point, and a test suite that runs against a fresh in-memory database per test. We finish by running it with curl, watching all eight tests pass, and walking through the lesson's stretch goals. Every line of code shown is pulled directly from the lesson — nothing invented.

Lessons covered in this video:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/javascript-mastery-path/level-3/11-project-rest-api-db/

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/javascript-mastery-path/level-3/11-project-rest-api-db/

beats.narration: Welcome to the Level 3 capstone of the JavaScript Mastery Path. Over the last ten modules you've picked up Express, SQLite, input validation, error handling, and testing. In this video we build one project that uses all of it: a Book Catalog REST API backed by a real database, step by step, file by file.

Step one is knowing what you're building. The goal is a Book Catalog API with full CRUD. Five endpoints: list all books, get one book by id, create a book, update a book, and delete a book. Creating and updating both run through validation, and a centralized error handler makes sure a bad request never crashes the server.

display.heading: Step 1: What You'll Build
display.subheading: A Book Catalog API — full CRUD

beats.narration: Here's the contract we're building to. Get books returns the whole list. Get books with an id returns one, or a 404. Post creates a book after validation. Put updates one after validation. Delete removes it and returns an empty 204. And a Jest plus supertest suite covers every one of those routes.

The whole thing is seven files. A package.json at the root. Inside src, we have db dot js for the database, booksController dot js for data access and validation, routes dot js for the Express router, app dot js to wire it together, and server dot js as the entry point. Tests live in their own folder.

display.code:
book-catalog-api/
    package.json
    src/
        db.js
        booksController.js
        routes.js
        app.js
        server.js
    test/
        books.test.js

beats.narration: The package.json is deliberately small. Type is module, so we use import syntax everywhere. Two scripts: start runs the server, test runs Jest. Two runtime dependencies, better-sqlite3 and express, and two dev dependencies, jest and supertest. That's the entire toolchain for a working, tested API.

db dot js exports one function, createDb. It takes a filename, defaulting to catalog dot db, opens a better-sqlite3 database, and turns on write-ahead logging mode for better concurrency. Then it runs a create table if not exists for books, with an auto-incrementing id, a required title and author, and an optional year.

Notice the filename is a parameter, not a hardcoded string. That one choice is what makes this testable. The running app passes catalog dot db, a real file on disk. The tests pass colon memory colon, an in-memory database that vanishes when the process exits. Same schema, same logic, and the tests never touch your real data.

The controller is a factory: give it a database, get back an object of functions. Up top it prepares five SQL statements once — insert, select all, select by id, update, and delete. Preparing them a single time and reusing them is both faster and safer than building query strings on every request.

validateBook collects errors into an array instead of throwing on the first problem, so the client sees everything that's wrong at once. Title and author must be non-empty strings. Year, if it's provided, must be an integer. There's a partial flag: in partial mode, only the fields actually present get checked, which is exactly what an update needs.

The rest are thin wrappers. listBooks returns every row. getBook fetches one by id. createBook inserts, then immediately reads the new row back using lastInsertRowid, so the response includes the generated id. updateBook merges incoming fields over the existing ones. deleteBook returns true only if a row actually changed.

routes dot js builds an Express router and wires each HTTP verb to a controller call. The list route is one line — return listBooks as JSON. The get-one route converts the id param to a number, and if the controller returns nothing, it replies 404 with a JSON error instead of undefined.

Post validates first; if the errors array isn't empty it returns 400 with the list, otherwise it creates and returns 201. Put does both checks — 404 if the book doesn't exist, 400 if the partial validation fails — then updates. Delete returns 204 with an empty body on success, or 404 if nothing was removed.

Every route handler is wrapped in try-catch, and the catch calls next with the error. It doesn't handle the failure there — it hands it off. That keeps each route focused on the happy path, and sends every unexpected error to one place: the error handler in app dot js.

app dot js creates the Express app and stacks middleware in order. First, express dot json to parse request bodies. Then a tiny logger that prints the method and URL of every request. Then the books router, mounted at slash books. Order matters here — each piece runs top to bottom.

After the router come two catch-alls. A 404 handler for any route that didn't match, so unknown URLs get a clean JSON message. And last of all, the four-argument error handler — that's the one next(error) feeds. It logs the stack and returns a generic 500, never leaking internals to the caller.

server dot js is the smallest file in the project, and that's the point. It creates a real database with the catalog dot db file, builds the app around it, reads a port from the environment or defaults to 3000, and starts listening. All the logic lives elsewhere, already tested.

The tests import createDb and createApp directly — there's no running server. A beforeEach hook builds a fresh in-memory database and a new app before every single test, so tests are fully isolated and never share state. The first test checks that getting books from an empty database returns an empty array.

supertest drives real HTTP requests against the app. One test posts a full book and expects 201, with a matching body and a defined id. Another posts a book with no title and expects 400, with the errors array containing the exact message about title being required. Happy path and failure path, side by side.

The update test creates a book, then sends a put with only a new title, and asserts the title changed while the author stayed untouched — that's the partial-update behavior, verified. The delete test removes a book, expects 204, then does a follow-up get and expects 404 to prove it's really gone.

Count them: empty list, create, reject a missing title, get by id, 404 on an unknown id, partial update, delete then confirm it's gone, and unknown routes return 404. Eight tests, and between them they exercise every endpoint and every error branch we wrote.
To run it for real: npm install, then npm start. The server comes up and logs that it's listening on localhost 3000. From here it's a normal Node process talking to a real SQLite file on disk.

display.output: Book Catalog API listening on http://localhost:3000

beats.narration: A plain get on books returns an empty array to start. Post a book with a JSON body and the right content-type header, and the API responds with the created record — id one, plus the title, author, and year you sent. That's the full create round-trip against a real database.

display.code:
curl http://localhost:3000/books

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/books \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","year":1965}'

beats.narration: And npm test runs the whole suite. Eight checks, all green, in a fraction of a second, because the in-memory database needs no setup and no teardown between tests.

display.output:
PASS  test/books.test.js
 ✓ GET /books starts empty
 ✓ POST /books creates a book
 ✓ POST /books rejects a missing title
 ✓ GET /books/:id returns a created book
 ✓ GET /books/:id returns 404 for an unknown id
 ✓ PUT /books/:id updates only the provided fields
 ✓ DELETE /books/:id removes the book
 ✓ unknown routes return 404

beats.narration: That's a complete REST API — routed, validated, error-handled, backed by a real database, and covered by tests that prove every route behaves. This is the shape of the backend services you'll build on the job, just with a smaller data model.

display.heading: It Works
display.subheading: a real service, end to end

beats.narration: The lesson leaves you five ways to push further. Add an author query filter and pagination to the list route. Add a second authors table with a foreign key from books, and a route for one author's books. Add API-key middleware protecting the write routes, with a test asserting 401 when the key is missing.

Then two bigger swaps: replace the hand-written validation with zod schemas, and replace SQLite with MongoDB — changing only the controller, while the routes and tests stay exactly the same. That last one shows you just how cleanly this layering isolates the data layer from everything else.

If you built this alongside the video, you've done something real — a full CRUD service from an empty folder, with a test suite that actually proves it. The lesson says it plainly: finishing this project means you're ready for Level 4, Master. Take the win and keep climbing.
The complete lesson, with every file in full and the stretch-goal links, is on screen now. Build it once by following along, then build it again from memory — that's when it really sticks.
